Honestly I'd be surprised if the Moon can be seen right now, but give me your honest estimate anyway.

I'm in Quito, Ecuador at 2026-07-14 07:19 -05 (UTC-0500) (2026-07-14T12:19:00Z in UTC), at latitude -0.1807 degrees and longitude -78.4678 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 13.738 degrees and its azimuth is 67.661 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 10.484 degrees and its azimuth is 65.013 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 0.09 percent illuminated, 3.445 degrees from the Sun, and 359152.1 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

No—realistically, you would not be able to spot it with unaided eyes.

The Moon is only **0.09% illuminated** and merely **3.45° from the Sun**, while the Sun is already **13.7° above the horizon**. The extremely thin crescent would have extraordinarily low contrast against the bright daylight sky and would also be overwhelmed by glare from the nearby Sun. Even though the Moon is geometrically above the horizon, atmospheric scattering at its **10.5° altitude** makes detection still harder.

My honest estimate is that unaided-eye visibility is **effectively zero** under these conditions—well below 1%, and probably closer to “not physically plausible” than merely difficult. Do not try to search with binoculars or a telescope this close to the Sun unless the Sun is securely blocked and proper solar-safety procedures are used.
